grammar.title: Present simple x continuous: além do básico
grammar.explanation_pt:
Você já sabe o básico: simple = rotina/fatos; continuous = agora/temporário. No B1+, acrescente:

**Present continuous para tendências e mudanças em andamento:**
"More people **are working** from home." / "Salaries **are rising**." / "The job market **is changing** fast."

**Present simple para estados permanentes e opiniões:**
"I **believe** that work should have purpose." / "This job **requires** patience."

**Verbos com dois sentidos** — são stative num sentido e de ação em outro:
- **think**: "I **think** it's a good idea" (opinião = simple) x "I**'m thinking** about quitting" (processo de pensar = continuous)
- **have**: "She **has** two jobs" (posse) x "She**'s having** a hard time" (experiência)
- **see**: "I **see** what you mean" (entender) x "I**'m seeing** a client at 3" (encontrar)
- **feel**: "I **feel** that..." (opinião) x "I**'m feeling** tired today" (sensação agora — ambos possíveis)
- **be**: "He **is** rude" (característica) x "He**'s being** rude" (comportamento temporário, agora)

**Always + continuous** = hábito irritante: "My boss **is always changing** deadlines!"

rows: I think remote work is better.
I'm thinking of applying for the job.

examples.en: More and more companies are offering four-day weeks.
examples.pt: Cada vez mais empresas estão oferecendo semanas de quatro dias.

examples.en: I'm thinking about volunteering on weekends.
examples.pt: Estou pensando em fazer trabalho voluntário nos fins de semana.

examples.en: My colleague is always taking credit for my ideas!

grammar.tip_pt: Para falar de **mudanças graduais**, combine continuous com **get / become / increase / decrease / more and more**: "Housing **is getting more expensive**."

reading.title: The meaning of work
reading.text: For decades, the typical career path was simple: study, get a stable job, climb the career ladder and retire. Today, many workers are questioning that model. Surveys in several countries suggest that a large number of employees — especially younger ones — are prepared to leave a job that doesn't match their values. Researchers who study job satisfaction say that money matters, but only up to a point. Once people earn enough to live comfortably, other factors become more important: autonomy (control over how you work), mastery (the feeling that you're improving) and purpose (the sense that your work matters to others). Interestingly, purpose doesn't require a "heroic" job. Hospital cleaners who see their role as helping patients recover often report high satisfaction. In other words, meaning doesn't only come from what we do, but from how we think about what we do.

writing.model: In my opinion, purpose and salary are both important, but purpose becomes more important once you earn enough to live comfortably. Today, more and more people are leaving well-paid jobs because they don't feel their work matters. I understand them. grammar.title: Verb + object + infinitive / make & let
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B1 você viu **verbo + -ing** e **verbo + to**. Agora, o padrão com **objeto** (a pessoa que recebe a ação):

**verbo + objeto + to + verbo**
want, ask, tell, expect, encourage, allow, persuade, remind, advise, teach, need, would like
- "My manager **wants me to lead** the project."
- "She **asked us to arrive** early."
- "My teacher **encouraged me to apply**."
- "They don't **allow employees to use** their phones."

⚠️ Em português dizemos "quero **que você** venha"; em inglês **nunca** use "that" aqui: ❌ "I want that you come" ✅ "I want **you to come**."

**make / let + objeto + verbo base (sem to):**
- **make** = obrigar, fazer com que: "My first boss **made me redo** the report three times."
- **let** = deixar, permitir: "My company **lets us work** from anywhere."
- (allow = let, mas com to: "They **allow us to work**...")

**Adjetivo + preposição + -ing:**
good **at**, capable **of**, keen **on**, interested **in**, used **to**, committed **to**, responsible **for**, tired **of**
- "She's **capable of managing** a big team." / "I'm **committed to improving** my English."

rows: want, ask, tell, encourage, allow, expect
They asked me to stay late.

grammar.tip_pt: **Let me** + verbo é uma expressão muito útil: "**Let me** check" (deixa eu ver), "**Let me** explain", "**Let me** know" (me avisa).

lines.en: People see the TV shows and think being a chef is glamorous. It isn't. My first boss made me clean the kitchen floor every night for six months before he let me cook anything. reading.title: Grit: the secret ingredient?
reading.text: Why do some people succeed while others with the same talent give up? Psychologist Angela Duckworth spent years studying this question with groups as different as military cadets, salespeople and children in spelling competitions. Her answer was a quality she called "grit": a combination of passion and perseverance for long-term goals. According to her research, grit was often a better predictor of success than talent or IQ. Gritty people aren't necessarily the most intelligent; they're the ones who keep going after failure. The good news is that grit can be developed. Parents and teachers can encourage children to finish what they start, let them experience small failures, and teach them to see mistakes as part of learning. Some critics argue that the concept is too similar to older ideas like conscientiousness, but the message remains popular: talent is important, but effort counts twice.

grammar.title: Used to / would / be & get used to
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Used to + verbo base** → hábitos ou estados do passado que **não são mais verdade**:
- "I **used to** play video games every night." (não jogo mais)
- "There **used to** be a cinema here."
- Negativa: "I **didn't use to** like coffee." (sem -d!) · Pergunta: "**Did** you **use to** live here?"

**Would + verbo base** → **ações** repetidas no passado (estilo nostálgico, narrativo). **Não** funciona com estados:
- "Every summer, we **would** go to the beach and **would** stay for weeks." ✅
- "I would have long hair." ❌ (estado → "I **used to** have long hair")

**Be used to + -ing / substantivo** → **estar acostumado**:
- "I**'m used to** wak**ing** up early." / "She **isn't used to** the cold."

**Get used to + -ing / substantivo** → **acostumar-se** (processo):
- "I**'m getting used to** speak**ing** English at work." / "You'll **get used to** it."

**Narrar a origem de algo:** past continuous (cenário) + simple past (eventos) + used to (como era antes):
"Before streaming, people **used to** buy CDs. One day, a student **was looking** for a way to share music and **created** a website. It **spread** quickly..."

reading.title: From fad to mainstream
reading.text: Why do some ideas disappear after a few months while others change the world? Sociologist Everett Rogers studied this question in the 1960s and developed a theory called the "diffusion of innovations". According to Rogers, new ideas spread through a population in stages. First come the innovators, a tiny group who love taking risks. Next, the early adopters try the idea and, crucially, tell others about it. Only after that does the majority follow — first the "early majority", then the more skeptical "late majority". Finally, the "laggards" accept the change, often reluctantly. Smartphones followed this pattern: in 2007 they were expensive gadgets for tech fans; a decade later, even grandparents were sending voice messages. Fads, on the other hand, usually never get past the early adopters. The difference? Real innovations solve a problem people actually have.

writing.model: Twenty years ago, people in Brazil didn't use to drink craft beer — most bars sold the same three or four brands. Then, in the early 2000s, a few homebrewers in the South started experimenting with new recipes in their garages. Some of these friends were early adopters: they began to ask for more, and small breweries opened. grammar.title: Indirect questions
grammar.explanation_pt:
**Perguntas indiretas** soam mais **educadas e profissionais**. Começam com uma expressão introdutória e usam a **ordem de afirmativa** (sujeito + verbo), **sem do/does/did**:

**Expressões introdutórias:**
- Could you tell me...? / Can you tell me...?
- Do you know...? / Do you have any idea...?
- I was wondering... / I'd like to know...
- Would you mind telling me...?

**Transformação:**
- "What **does the job involve**?" → "Could you tell me what **the job involves**?"
- "When **will I hear** from you?" → "Do you know when **I'll hear** from you?"
- "Why **did she leave**?" → "I was wondering why **she left**."

**Perguntas de sim/não** usam **if** ou **whether**:
- "**Is** remote work possible?" → "Could you tell me **if/whether** remote work **is** possible?"

Repare na pontuação: se a frase introdutória é uma afirmação ("I was wondering..."), termina com **ponto**, não interrogação.

**No contexto de entrevista**, perguntas indiretas são ótimas para fazer perguntas sensíveis com elegância: "I was wondering **what the salary range is** for this position."

lines.en: I've interviewed hundreds of Brazilian candidates, and they're usually excellent — friendly, creative and hard-working. But I often see three mistakes. First, they're too modest. reading.title: The questions behind the questions
reading.text: Most interview questions aren't really about what they seem to ask. "Tell me about yourself" isn't an invitation to share your life story; the interviewer wants a short, relevant summary that explains why you're right for the job. "Why do you want to leave your current job?" is testing your professionalism: criticizing your current boss is a red flag, even if your boss is terrible. "Where do you see yourself in five years?" checks whether your goals match what the company can offer — and whether you're likely to stay. And the famous "What's your biggest weakness?" is about self-awareness: the worst answers are "I don't have any" or the cliché "I'm a perfectionist" without any example. Experts suggest preparing three or four short stories about your experience that you can adapt to different questions. When you understand the question behind the question, you can answer what the interviewer really wants to know.
